segments.say: It's ten past two in the morning, and Marta is wide awake. The street party ended hours ago. The tables are folded, the paper lanterns are down, and her bedroom is quiet. But her mind is still at the party, stuck on one small, ordinary moment. A man walked up, smiled, and said her name. And she had no idea what his was.

A quick word about Marta. She's imagined. She's a person we've pictured together to keep us company through tonight's ideas. She's in her early forties, she works as a physiotherapist, and she lives on a street where people still wave from their front steps. She's friendly, a little forgetful, and completely ordinary. We borrow her because her night might look a lot like one of yours.

Here's the moment. A man in a linen shirt crossed the street party with a paper cup in his hand and said, Marta! Great to see you! And she knew him. Of course she knew him. He's the man with the lemon-yellow bicycle, the one who once spent an afternoon fixing her garden gate. She said, hey, you! with the warmest smile she could manage, and hoped that would be enough.

show.cap: The man with the yellow bicycle

segments.say: Here's the strange part. She could have told you almost everything about him. His daughter plays the violin, badly and bravely, through an open window every Thursday. He grows tomatoes on his balcony. He once lent her a ladder. But the one small thing that people actually say out loud, his name, was a smooth blank wall. It felt like reaching for a light switch in a familiar room and finding nothing there.

show.cap: A blank where a name should be

segments.say: So here's the question Marta is asking the ceiling, and maybe you've asked it too. How can a mind hold so much about a person, and still lose the one word that belongs to him? It feels like a failure. It feels a little embarrassing. And at two in the morning, it feels like it matters far more than it should.

show.text: I know his face, his bicycle and his ladder. Why not his name?

segments.say: If this has ever happened to you, you're in enormous company. Meeting someone you clearly know, and being unable to produce their name, is one of the most familiar small frustrations of being human. It doesn't mean your memory is breaking. It doesn't mean you weren't paying attention to your neighbours. It means you have a face-loving brain, and that brain does things in a very particular order.

show.cap: You are in very large company

segments.say: Here's where we're going tonight. Why faces feel so easy. A special region of the brain for faces. A single neuron that fires for a single person. The route a face has to travel before it becomes a name. The strange case of Baker and baker. Why names are harder to learn than other facts. The tip of the tongue. What time and age change. People who cannot recognise faces, and people who never forget one. And what truly helps.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore

segments.say: Before we start, a promise. There's nothing to memorise tonight, and no test at the end. Nobody here will tell you to try harder, or to pay more attention, or to use a trick with a funny rhyme. We're just going to be curious about how this works. And the second half of the night is a long, slow wind-down, so if you drift off along the way, that's the plan working.
Let's begin with a kind of tally, the one Marta is quietly keeping in the dark.

Marta decides to count everything she knows about him, as a kind of detective exercise. He lives at number fourteen. He's about fifty. He has a dog with one floppy ear. He sings along, a little out of tune, to the radio in his garden. He laughs with his whole face. She keeps adding to the list, and it keeps getting longer. The one item that never appears is the one she's searching for.

Here's the list as it stands at ten past two. His face. His yellow bicycle. His daughter's violin. His tomatoes. His laugh. And then, at the bottom, his name, which is still blank. Notice that the blank isn't empty because she knows nothing about him. It's empty in the middle of a great deal of knowing. That's what makes it so odd, and so interesting.

Look at Marta's room for a moment. A small lamp, turned low. Curtains half drawn. A folded blanket at the foot of the bed. It's one of the calmest rooms you could picture. And inside it, a mind is turning over a single word that it can't find, like someone patting every pocket of a coat for keys that were in the other coat all along.

show.cap: A quiet room, a busy mind

segments.say: At the party, Marta did what almost everyone does. She smiled a little wider. She said, how have you been? instead of using any name at all. She asked about the tomatoes, because that was safe. She even introduced him to her sister as, this is, um, my neighbour, and the man gamely filled in his own name. Marta didn't catch it. The music was loud, and a dog was barking.

show.cap: She did what we all do

segments.say: And now, in the dark, the memory of that moment has come back. She hears herself say, this is, um. She remembers the half second where the man's smile held still, waiting. It wasn't unkind. It was just a little pause. But at two in the morning, a little pause can feel like a very big one, and she's replaying it again and again.

Here's a small thought to keep with you tonight. Knowing someone and naming someone are two different jobs, and the brain does them in different places and at different times. When the second job fails, the first one is usually still working perfectly. Marta didn't forget her neighbour. She forgot a label. And as we'll see, those are very different things.

show.text: Knowing someone and naming someone are two different jobs.

segments.say: The street party was her sister's idea. Every autumn, the neighbours close off the lane, drag out their tables, string up lights and bring far more food than anyone can eat. Marta likes it, mostly. She likes the cheese straws and the children chasing each other with sparklers that aren't really sparklers. What she finds harder is the talking, especially the hundred small greetings of people who all seem to know exactly who she is.

Most of those greetings were easy. The woman from the bakery, with her bright scarf. The retired teacher who always asks about her knee. The two brothers from the end house, who look so alike that she's never been sure which is which, though she knows both their names perfectly well. Face after face, and name after name, arriving without a thought. It was only one name, out of dozens, that failed to show up.

That's worth noticing, because in the dark it feels like a defeat. In fact, it was one miss among a great many hits. Marta recognised dozens of faces that evening, and she named most of them. But the mind doesn't keep score of what went right. It's drawn, as minds are, to the single place where something didn't, and it picks at it all night long.

Perhaps that's one of the quiet truths of a night like this. The mind counts the miss and forgets the hits. A hundred easy recognitions pass without a flicker of notice, and one stuck name takes over the whole evening. It's not that the name was important. It's that the mind has a habit of attending to what's unfinished.

show.text: The mind counts the miss and forgets the hits.

segments.say: Before she lies back down, Marta makes herself a small promise. She won't look him up. She won't ask her sister, at least not tonight. She'll just let the question sit and see what the mind does with it. And that, as it turns out, is a very good experiment, one we'll come back to when we reach the end of the story.

So let's be clear about what tonight is not. It's not a lecture about paying attention. It's not advice to carry a notebook of names. It's not a cure for a feeling that every human being has had. It's a calm, curious look at one of the most ordinary mysteries of memory, with a little science and a lot of time.
So let's begin where Marta's night began, with a face that her mind recognised instantly.

Before we go there, take one slow breath in, and let it out a little longer than you breathed in. Marta does the same. She turns onto her side and looks at the thin line of lamplight under the door. The missing name is still missing. But it's a little quieter now that she's curious about it. And curiosity is a very good place to start.
